lead: Real loads are not one resistor and one capacitor. A gate drives a tree of wires and transistor stacks, each piece with its own resistance and capacitance. The Elmore delay model gives one time constant for any node of such an RC tree by a simple rule: for every capacitor, multiply it by the resistance its charging current shares with the path to the node, and add. Some syllabi call this Elmore's constant. It is quick enough to use by hand on a series transistor stack or a branching wire, and timing tools use it as their first estimate of wire delay.
prereq: You need: the RC delay idea in switching characteristics and the wire models in interconnect parameters.

blocks.text: An RC tree has one input (the driver) and resistors that branch out without loops, with a capacitor from every node to ground. Let R<sub>ik</sub> be the resistance of the part of the path from the input to node i that is shared with the path from the input to node k. The Elmore delay at node i is:
τDi = Σk CkRik Here the sum runs over every capacitor Ck in the tree, including those on side branches. A side-branch capacitor sees only the resistance up to where its branch leaves the path.

Mathematically τ<sub>Di</sub> is the first moment of the node's impulse response, the average arrival time of its edge. For a single RC it equals RC exactly, and the 50% delay is 0.69RC. For a tree, 0.69τ<sub>D</sub> is the usual estimate of the 50% delay. (Some textbooks fold the 0.69 into an effective resistance and quote the Elmore delay itself as the delay; either way, keep one convention through a problem.)

items: Draw the tree with every resistor and node capacitor.
Mark the path from the driver to the node you care about.
For each capacitor, find where its own path leaves the marked path and add the resistance up to that point.
Multiply, add the products for τ<sub>D</sub>, and take 0.69τ<sub>D</sub> as the delay.

blocks.text: For an RC ladder (a chain) the rule becomes: each capacitor is multiplied by all the resistance between it and the driver. With N equal sections of R/N and C/N:

blocks.where: R and C are the totals of the line. For N = 1 this is RC; as N grows it falls towards RC/2.

blocks.text: So the Elmore delay of a distributed wire is RC/2, against the exact 50% delay of 0.38RC. The rule overestimates a little, and it is never optimistic at the far end of a tree, which is why it is safe for a first pass. A driver of resistance R<sub>d</sub> feeding a wire R<sub>w</sub>, C<sub>w</sub> and a load C<sub>L</sub> gives τ<sub>D</sub> = R<sub>d</sub>(C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>L</sub>) + R<sub>w</sub>(C<sub>w</sub>/2 + C<sub>L</sub>).

A conducting transistor is a resistor, and every internal node of a stack has diffusion capacitance. In a three-input NAND the output falls through three series nMOS. Number the nodes from the output down: the output node C<sub>out</sub> sees all three resistances, the node below it two, the one below that one. The output capacitance therefore dominates, but internal nodes add delay too.

This gives two design rules. Place the input that arrives last on the transistor nearest the output: by then the lower internal nodes are already discharged, so the late edge has less charge to move. And keep stacks short: τ<sub>D</sub> of an n-high stack grows roughly as n², one reason gates with more than four series transistors are split.

examples.question: A driver of 1 kΩ feeds node 1 (20 fF). From node 1, one branch of 2 kΩ goes to node 2 (30 fF) and continues through 1 kΩ to node 4 (40 fF); another branch of 3 kΩ goes to node 3 (10 fF). Find the Elmore delay and the estimated 50% delay at node 4 and at node 3.
steps: Path to node 4: 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ, 1 kΩ. Shared resistances: C<sub>1</sub> sees 1 kΩ; C<sub>2</sub> sees 1 + 2 = 3 kΩ; C<sub>3</sub> leaves at node 1, so 1 kΩ; C<sub>4</sub> sees 4 kΩ.
Path to node 3: 1 kΩ, 3 kΩ. C<sub>1</sub>: 1 kΩ; C<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>4</sub> leave at node 1: 1 kΩ each; C<sub>3</sub>: 4 kΩ.
50% delays: 0.69 × 280 = 193 ps at node 4 and 0.69 × 130 = 90 ps at node 3.
examples.answer: τ<sub>D4</sub> = 280 ps (about 193 ps to 50%) and τ<sub>D3</sub> = 130 ps (about 90 ps).

examples.question: A NAND3 pull-down has three nMOS of 2 kΩ each when on. The output node has 30 fF; the two internal nodes have 5 fF each. All internal nodes start charged. Find the Elmore delay of the falling output. How much of it is due to the internal nodes?
steps: Name the nodes from the bottom: x<sub>1</sub> (above the lowest transistor), x<sub>2</sub>, then the output.
x<sub>1</sub> discharges through 2 kΩ, x<sub>2</sub> through 4 kΩ, the output through 6 kΩ.
τ<sub>D</sub> = 5 fF × 2 kΩ + 5 fF × 4 kΩ + 30 fF × 6 kΩ = 10 + 20 + 180 = 210 ps.

Internal nodes contribute 30 ps of the 210 ps, 14%. If the lower inputs were already high so x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> were at 0 V before the top input rises, only 180 ps would remain: the reason to put the latest input at the top.
examples.answer: τ<sub>D</sub> = 210 ps, a 50% delay of about 145 ps; the internal nodes add 30 ps (14%).

traps: Multiplying a side-branch capacitor by the whole path resistance. It sees only the resistance shared with the path, up to the branch point.
Leaving out the capacitors on branches that do not lead to the node. Every capacitor in the tree is in the sum.
Quoting τ<sub>D</sub> as the 50% delay in one step and 0.69τ<sub>D</sub> in the next. State the convention once.
Using RC for a distributed wire. The Elmore delay of a uniform line is RC/2.
Putting the late-arriving input at the bottom of a stack. It belongs nearest the output.

quiz.q: State the Elmore delay formula for node i of an RC tree.
quiz.a: τ<sub>Di</sub> = Σ C<sub>k</sub>R<sub>ik</sub>, where R<sub>ik</sub> is the resistance shared by the paths from the input to node i and to node k.

quiz.q: Why does a capacitor on a side branch still slow down node i?
quiz.a: Its charging current flows through the resistors it shares with the path to node i, so it lowers the voltage at node i while it charges.

quiz.q: A 5 mm wire has R = 1375 Ω and C = 1.015 pF. Find its Elmore delay with 1 section and with 5 equal sections.
quiz.a: N = 1: RC = 1.40 ns. N = 5: RC × 6/10 = 0.84 ns. The limit is RC/2 = 0.70 ns.

quiz.q: A driver of 4 kΩ drives a wire of 500 Ω and 100 fF into a 20 fF gate. Find τ<sub>D</sub> at the gate.
Why does the delay of an n-high series stack grow about as n²?
quiz.a: Its resistance grows as n and so does the number of internal capacitances, and each node sees the resistance below it, so the sum grows roughly as n².

quiz.q: In the NAND3 example the output load rises from 30 fF to 60 fF. Recompute τ<sub>D</sub> and say which design change helps most.
quiz.a: τ<sub>D</sub> = 10 + 20 + 360 = 390 ps. The output term dominates, so widening all three nMOS (lowering each 2 kΩ) helps most; reordering inputs saves at most the 30 ps of the internal nodes.

quiz.q: Is the Elmore delay an optimistic or pessimistic estimate for the far end of a distributed wire? Explain with numbers.
quiz.a: Pessimistic: it gives RC/2 = 0.5RC, while the exact 50% delay is 0.38RC, so it overstates by about 30%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Elmore's 1948 paper was about amplifier delay; it was applied to MOS RC trees in the 1980s. Timing tools now match more moments of the response (AWE and its successors) and model the gate output as a current source. Search next for asymptotic waveform evaluation, effective capacitance and current-source delay models.
